title: A review-gated agent team with a merge gate
summary: Each task gets its own agent session, every pull request gets a review, and a tiered gate decides when it merges. Over 1,200 pull requests have merged this way.

stat.label: merge volume rose sharply once a deterministic gate, not me, decided what could merge

sections.heading: Problem
paragraphs: Each task gets its own agent session, and no session approves its own work. That rule is easy to state and easy to break, so the question was how to keep it true while one person runs a platform across many repos.

sections.heading: Testing the control
paragraphs: Before this gate, I built and retired an unattended agent that opened draft pull requests from labelled tickets. Its safety rested on one claim: the GitHub App it used could not merge its own pull request. I tested the claim instead of assuming it. As the real App, against two throwaway branches, the merge call returned 405 on the branch that required one review and 200 on an unprotected control, back to back. The control is what makes the 405 mean something: without it, a refusal looks the same as a broken credential.

I never enabled that agent's timer and retired it. Independent review, the merge gate above and one project thread per task replaced it. Reviews come from Codex first. When Codex stays silent for two hours, a local model reviews the low-risk tiers, and a Claude review agent covers a pull request the local model fails twice. Two rules outlived it: every pull request is reviewed before it merges, and no session merges its own work in the infrastructure repo.

sections.heading: What I built
paragraphs: An agent workflow where each task gets its own session, every pull request gets a review, and no session approves its own work. A session may merge its own PR only outside the infrastructure repo, and only after a separate review has cleared it.

A tiered gate decides who merges. A script scores each PR's blast radius from the files it touches. Tier 0 is prose. Tier 1 is code that runs nothing on merge. Tier 2 is everything else, such as infrastructure code and workflows. A merge bot with deterministic code merges tiers 0 and 1 after CI and a clean review. A separate merger handles tier 2 under the same gate. No model output widens what merges.

A PR waits when its review has a blocking finding, a check is red or skipped, or it has no checks. It also waits when it carries a hold label, asks to wait, or needs a hand step. A push voids the review of the old head, and the merge is pinned to the commit that was reviewed. After each merge, the bot reads the main branch back and expects the change to be there.

An unrecognised file path counts as tier 2, because the rules fail closed. Infrastructure changes run `validate` on PR, then `plan` and `apply` on merge. Credentials and destructive flags stay hand steps that no merge runs.

sections.heading: Workflows added since
paragraphs: Reviewer chain. Every pull request gets a review before it merges. A hosted reviewer goes first. After two hours of silence from it, a local model running on my own GPU reviews instead. When that model fails twice on the same pull request, a Claude subagent takes the review. The chain has one rule: a review that could not run is not a clean review.

Gated lab writes. An agent can ask my lab to apply a change, but a write waits on an approval environment where I am the only reviewer. Reads run without a tap. A merge that would destroy resources also waits on an approval, in place of an environment flag.

A tracker outbox. Many sessions share one tracker key, and the tracker's rate limit stopped all of them once. Now a session never calls the tracker. It adds one small file to a queue repository, a single job applies the queue at about 60 calls a minute, and the session reports the file's id, not "closed". An item counts as closed when its file has moved to the done folder and the mirror shows the state.
A merge desk. One deterministic desk merges pull requests by tier once the review is clean. Trust-boundary changes, such as workflows and secret-store bindings, wait for my word.

sections.heading: Result
paragraphs: Across the eight repositories in scope, 1,219 pull requests had merged by 13 November 2026, out of 1,284 opened. The week of 19 October was the first peak: 209 opened and 207 merged. The week after fell to 31 opened and 26 merged, and the week of 2 November reached 230 opened and 211 merged.

Weeks run Monday to Sunday in US Eastern time, and I read the counts from GitHub search. Most of these pull requests carry an agent author or footer, but that is a heuristic, because an agent's pull request can come from my own login. The swings show a peak is not a steady rate. Throughput is the measure here, not quality.

sections.heading: A failure that taught me
paragraphs: One day the secrets store sat sealed for most of a working day. The watcher that unsealed it ran on a laptop that had gone to sleep. The tracker reconcile job, which had gained a batch of calling repos the day before, reported success in every one while reconciling nothing. Its token step was set to continue, and the next step treated a missing token as a clean exit. A warning annotation does not colour a check.

Two other things stood out. The sibling reconcile job had hit the same error and failed loudly, because an earlier incident had already fixed it there. And the uptime monitor recorded every missed heartbeat for the sealed store, then told nobody, because none of its monitors had a notification channel attached.

The reconcile job now fails when it cannot get a token, and says why. The unseal watcher moved to an always-on machine and re-reads the seal status after it submits the key, so it exits non-zero if the store is still sealed. The recurring bug was a green check over work that never happened. In the status jobs I audited, each now fails non-zero and reports what it examined, not only what it found.

sections.heading: What I would do differently
paragraphs: Write the reporting rule before the first automation, not after the sixth bug. Six separate work items had the same shape: a job that could not authenticate, could not reach its target, or checked nothing, and reported success.
The rule that ended it is short. A failure path exits non-zero, and a check says what it examined, not only what it found. A gate that relaxes a check replaces the signal it removed.
